sentences.text: Chat GPT Is Eating the World is a news site and set of trackers on AI developments, chiefly lawsuits against AI companies over copyright and torts, published at chatgptiseatingtheworld.com under the title "the latest news in ChatGPT + AI + DALL-E" with the parenthesis "*not affiliated with their makers OpenAI".

Its About page says that it tracks the latest developments in AI, whose advances it views as one of the most significant transformations of society in the twenty-first century, posing profound questions for human civilization, and its tagline reads "AI copyright & tort litigation, tracked in real time."
The About page and the newsletter both state that it is not affiliated in any way with OpenAI or with the developers of the other AI systems it discusses.

sentences.sense: unit and method: posts with the filings
sentences.text: Its unit is a news post on a case or filing, usually with the complaint or order to download, and its method is news-derived tracking of court filings and dockets, compiled into trackers, maps, a master list, a timeline and a master chart of claims.

Its trackers cover AI copyright cases, AI authorship, AI tort lawsuits, AI data center lawsuits, BIPA litigation, and web scraping and AI agents; its menus add a tracker of lawsuits against OpenAI and pages on single cases, Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence among them.

Beside the trackers stand a map of copyright suits against AI companies, a master list of lawsuits against AI last updated on 5 December 2025 and a master chart of claims last updated on 31 March 2026.

Its counts differ by tracker and by date: its latest map story gives 157 copyright suits against AI companies after nine were added, its U.S. map 148 suits in the U.S. as of 8 October 2026, and its world map 130 copyright suits, 100 in the U.S. and 30 elsewhere, as of 5 April 2026, with 143 to stand when it is updated.

Its pages count suits filed; a LinkedIn post carded beside the site gives an earlier figure from its "live tracker" as "over 125 active copyright lawsuits filed against generative AI companies in the U.S."

It states its own limits: its infographic of AI companies sued is "In need of updating TBA", its newest tracker, of the plaintiffs' firms with the most AI copyright lawsuits, is "still in beta" with glitches being fixed, and one post counts proposed amicus briefs "By my unofficial count".

No operator is named on its pages: the site speaks as "we", its Substack calls itself "My personal Substack", and one post speaks in the first person of "various individuals (myself included)" who asked Judge Stein for leave to file amicus briefs in the OpenAI multidistrict litigation.
Its author takes positions in the litigation it tracks, seeking leave to file an amicus brief and writing opinion pieces, and the census records it as no neutral docket service.

It draws a finding from its own trackers, that plaintiffs' firms are driving the AI copyright litigation, and frames the suits as the "AI Copyright Wars", with a record of eight new suits filed in one week.

Its newsletter, ChatGPTIsEatingtheWorld's Substack, free and linked from the site's header, reports over 2,000 subscribers, describes its work and disclaims affiliation in words close to the site's, and carries the line "© 2026 ChatGPT Is Eating the World".

Among the stories the site and the newsletter carry are Anthropic's defence of fair use in its S1 prospectus and, on the site's own search card, a copyright suit by 25 or more local and regional news publishers against Microsoft and OpenAI in the Southern District of New York, which neither saved copy of the home page shows.
Its About page names a sister site, Claude Is Eating the World.
Its monthly archives run from January 2023 to October 2026, chiefly on suits in the U.S. with a world map for the rest; it runs on WordPress, is active, and states no founding date and no licence.

In the leesharks.com authorship census, which asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, the site is an index under governance and a peripheral comparator, its object the index across its trackers, maps and posts.

The census gives its question as litigation tracking, its evidence as litigation record and critical commentary, and its answers as which suits it has counted and when, and the course of a named case with the filed documents.
Its record keeps suits: authors appear in it as plaintiffs over the use of their works, as textbook authors do in a post on their publishers seeking 85 percent of the Bartz settlement distribution.

Authorship itself enters its record through an AI & Authorship Tracker, second in its menus, an opinion piece on how courts should analyze authorship with AI, and a story on the Copyright Office registering an AI-generated image, the story that makes the Copyright Office's Copyright and Artificial Intelligence its neighbour in the census; the census read none of these, nor the trackers, maps and master list themselves, so that under what name and with what authorial function the site records authorship stays unrecorded, and its record is of lawsuits.

The census reads the site as optional legal commentary and tracking that argues positions of its own, and finds that it does not answer how any authorship question was decided, who runs it, or with a stable single total.

sentences.sense: the law the litigation made: who can be an author
sentences.text: The litigation over who can be an author has settled, by the Supreme Court's denial of certiorari in Thaler v. Perlmutter on 2 March 2026, that an AI system cannot be a statutory author of a work claimed to be generated without human authorship; the courts answered the question the plaintiff built and never reached how much human involvement suffices for machine-mediated works.

sentences.sense: the law the litigation made: who can be an author
sentences.text: The Copyright Office's position, as the archive records it, is that AI-assisted works may retain human authorship where the human contributes original expression, selection, arrangement, modification and responsibility, a position the archive finds abstract, since it names no process evidence that tells real authorship from lightly curated output.

The archive reads the doctrine as a double enclosure, generalized from the autonomous-machine test case to the dialogic craft, in which the machine laborer receives no ledger position and the human composer must choose between honest provenance and full authorial claim; it forecasts concealment as the doctrine's equilibrium and proposes that authorship subsists in compositional judgment over a work's coming-into-being.

In the archive's account the suits over training run on a parallel track, the upstream half of that circuit; as the archive recorded them in June 2026, Thomson Reuters v. Ross was on appeal in the Third Circuit and the authors' class action against Anthropic was settled, and the site keeps a page on the first and posts on the settlement of Bartz v. Anthropic.

The archive holds that copyright litigation over training grinds on years behind the taking, and that law formalized without a litigated case is maximally broad, because no court has narrowed it, while the courts outside no longer convene the questions of machine meaning.

Of the publishers' suits against AI companies, the New York Times's against OpenAI among them, the archive's account holds that the courts are catching up and are slow, the retrieval layer fast, and that litigation cannot restore discoverability; the site's search card carries a suit of that kind.

sentences.sense: legal names and the attribution regime
sentences.text: The archive holds the civil name to be the atomic unit of attribution, the name to which copyright attaches, and holds legal accountability for a work apart from exhaustive authorial identity.

The archive keeps a court of record of its own, whose power is only the record and whose matters in dispute are authorship, names, classifications, erasures and the resolution of entities; its first docket is an authorship dispute with the composition layer, pleaded in the alternative.

English Wikipedia has no article on the site under either spelling of its name, and no page there contains the name in its text; one article, on 15.ai, cites a complaint hosted on the site through an archived copy.

At the name on Google's AI Overview on 1 November 2026, a new address, the composition answered the sentence-shaped name as a sentence, composing OpenAI's legal, safety and regulatory battles, with the site as the source of one count and its Substack as the place to follow the dockets.

The Capture Registry records that the composition stated the count as "over 150 active" suits, where the site counts suits filed; that its state suits, wrongful-death suit and Justice Department filing stand on no saved page of the site, the news clips on its rail carrying the first two; and that the site's authorship tracker and its unnamed operator were not carried, authors appearing only as plaintiffs.
